summary: Presents a generic key management API that can be used for IP Security and other network security services, letting key management programs talk to the part of the operating system that does the encryption.

eli5.summary: A standard way for a key-keeper program to hand secret keys to the part of the computer that locks and unlocks messages.

questions: how does the kernel get cryptographic keys
subtitle: A system call interface for managing cryptographic keys in the kernel.

tldr.problem: When an operating system kernel needs cryptographic keys to protect traffic, those keys must come from somewhere and be managed securely. Key management daemons running as user-space applications need a standardized way to deliver keys to the kernel.
tldr.mechanism: PF_KEY is a socket-based protocol family that lets trusted key management applications send and receive messages to the kernel's Security Association Database (SADB), creating, updating, retrieving, and deleting security associations that hold cryptographic keys and their parameters.
tldr.outcome: This became a widely adopted interface for IPsec key management on Unix-like systems, allowing different key management protocols (ISAKMP/Oakley, manual keying, GKMP) to use the same kernel interface.

today: RFC 2367 remains a widely implemented interface on BSD, Linux, and other Unix-like systems for IPsec key management. It is Informational, not a Standard, but it serves as the de facto standard for PF_KEY implementations in production systems.

sections.title: The Key Management Problem
sections.content:
IPsec and other network security protocols need cryptographic keys to encrypt and authenticate traffic, but where do those keys come from? In Unix-like systems, the kernel implements the fast cryptographic processing, but it should not be responsible for negotiating keys or managing policy. PF_KEY solves this by providing a socket-based API that lets trusted user-space key management daemons communicate with the kernel's Security Association Database (SADB).

A Security Association (SA) bundles together all the parameters needed for cryptography: the encryption key, the authentication key, the algorithms, the IP addresses, lifetime limits, and other configuration. PF_KEY lets applications create, store, retrieve, update, and delete these associations in the kernel.
sections.eli5: Imagine the kernel is a safe and a key-keeper program is a locksmith. The locksmith needs a way to tell the safe 'put this key away' or 'give me the key for addresses A to B'. PF_KEY is their telephone line.

sections.title: How Key Management Daemons Use PF_KEY
sections.content:
A key management daemon, such as an ISAKMP/Oakley or SKIP implementation, runs as a privileged user-space process. When the kernel needs a new Security Association for an outbound packet, it sends an SADB_ACQUIRE message to all registered key management daemons. The daemon reads this request (including its sequence number), negotiates keys with a remote peer over the network using its own protocol, then sends an SADB_ADD or SADB_UPDATE message back to the kernel with the new SA.

The kernel maintains the SADB internally. When a packet matches an SA, the kernel retrieves it (via an internal interface, not PF_KEY) and applies the specified cryptography. When an SA's lifetime expires, the kernel sends an SADB_EXPIRE message to remind the daemon to renegotiate.
sections.eli5: When your computer needs a new key, it asks the key-keeper 'I need a key for talking to Bob.' The key-keeper calls Bob's key-keeper, they decide on a secret key together, then the key-keeper tells the computer 'here it is, use this one.' Later, when the key gets old, the computer reminds the key-keeper to get a new one.

sections.title: Message Structure and Operations
sections.content:
All PF_KEY messages start with a 16-byte base header containing a version field (must be set to PF_KEY_V2), a message type, an error code, a Security Association type (for IPsec ESP, AH, or other protocols), a length field, a sequence number for matching requests to responses, and a process ID. After the base header come optional extension headers for the Security Association itself, lifetime parameters, addresses, keys, algorithm proposals, identities, and sensitivity labels.

Message types include SADB_GETSPI (request a new SPI identifier from the kernel), SADB_UPDATE and SADB_ADD (store an SA), SADB_DELETE (remove an SA), SADB_GET (retrieve an SA), SADB_DUMP (list all SAs, mainly for debugging), SADB_FLUSH (delete all SAs of a type), and SADB_REGISTER (announce that this daemon handles a particular SA type).
sections.eli5: Every message is like a letter with a standard envelope (the header), and then you can attach different kinds of pages depending on what you're saying. The envelope says who you are and what you want; the pages say 'here's the key' or 'here's the address' or 'here's how long this should last.'

sections.title: Privilege and Trust Requirements
sections.content:
PF_KEY is a privileged interface: only trusted processes (typically running as root on Unix systems, or with the 'key management privilege' on multi-level security systems) can open a PF_KEY socket. If an unprivileged user could manipulate keys and security associations, they could decrypt or forge traffic, breaking all security. The RFC emphasizes that the overall security depends on the operating system's ability to enforce privilege boundaries, the correctness of the PF_KEY implementation, and the correctness of the key management applications themselves.

Security policy (deciding which traffic needs protection and how) is deliberately separate from PF_KEY. The RFC leaves policy configuration to other mechanisms, so that different policies can share the same key management infrastructure.
sections.eli5: Only the computer's administrator (with a special password or key) can talk to the key manager. If a regular user could send fake keys, they could trick the computer into using weak encryption or give them the real encryption keys. So this is guarded very carefully.

sections.title: Common Usage Patterns
sections.content:
For a simple IPsec deployment, a key management daemon registers itself with the kernel via SADB_REGISTER, announcing it will handle ESP and AH security associations. When the kernel needs a new SA (because a packet requires protection and no SA exists), it sends SADB_ACQUIRE. The daemon gets an SPI (Security Parameters Index, a unique identifier) via SADB_GETSPI, negotiates keys with the remote end using ISAKMP, then sends SADB_UPDATE to populate the SA with keys and algorithms.

For proxy or firewall scenarios, the SAs may cover traffic between the firewall and an external peer, while protecting traffic from internal hosts. The RFC also shows how a routing protocol like OSPF running in user space (e.g., a routing daemon) can request and retrieve SAs via SADB_GET and SADB_ACQUIRE messages, even though the kernel does not implement the routing protocol's security itself.
sections.eli5: A key manager says 'I can do IPsec.' The computer says 'I need a key for Alice.' The key manager talks to Alice's computer, they agree on a secret key, the key manager tells the computer 'use this key for Alice,' and now they can talk securely.
